tabs.title: Responsiveness and Pressure
tabs.description: Interpret how read receipts alter expectations.

tabs.title: Benefits and Limits
tabs.description: Evaluate arguments for and against read receipts.

questions.q: Why does the author describe reading a message as a kind of promise?
choices: It legally binds the recipient to complete a task.
It guarantees that the sender understands the answer.
A read receipt can make the recipient feel obliged to answer immediately.
It proves that the message concerns an emergency.
questions.explanation: The author connects blue ticks with a clock and expectations after reading.

questions.q: What is the significance of rewarding the first worker to answer a late-night shift request?
choices: Availability becomes an informal condition of being seen as reliable.
The manager has formally abolished contracted hours.
All staff have equal opportunities to answer while asleep.
The extra shifts are assigned by an independent lottery.
questions.explanation: The example shows hidden incentives without a written duty to stay online.

questions.q: What makes unspoken rules about response times particularly difficult?
choices: Every social group follows exactly the same convention.
The rules are always displayed beside a read receipt.
A delayed answer necessarily shows deliberate disrespect.
People can break expectations that they did not know existed.
questions.explanation: Newcomers learn unwritten rules through mistakes and conflict.

questions.q: Which benefit of read receipts does the writer genuinely acknowledge?
choices: They show whether the recipient is emotionally ready to reply.
They may confirm that an important emergency message has been seen.
They reveal why a response has not arrived.
They prevent people from ignoring inconvenient messages entirely.
questions.explanation: The author concedes that knowledge of reception can matter in emergencies.

questions.q: What is the central weakness in equating reading with availability?
choices: All messages need long thoughtful replies.
Only people at work can understand short messages.
Seeing words gives no reliable information about the capacity to respond.
The sender knows exactly what the recipient is doing.
questions.explanation: The text distinguishes reading from the time, energy or knowledge required to reply.

questions.q: Why is switching read receipts off not necessarily a free choice?
choices: Other people may interpret the disabled setting as a social statement.
The setting can never be changed on a phone.
Switching it off automatically deletes group chats.
The recipient will no longer be able to read messages.
questions.explanation: The writer points out that disabling receipts may itself be meaningful to others.

questions.q: Why do disagreements over response time often emerge indirectly?
choices: The technology blocks users from describing their expectations.
All conflicts disappear when emojis are used.
Group members are forbidden from speaking face-to-face.
Unspoken expectations encourage hints rather than open negotiation.
questions.explanation: Short replies and deliberate delays can convey resentment about invisible rules.

questions.q: What is the value of agreeing that club members need not reply after ten?
choices: It means urgent situations can never arise.
It removes uncertainty by setting a shared boundary in advance.
It makes all messaging outside school illegal.
It guarantees that every person will read messages at ten.
questions.explanation: The writer suggests making expectations explicit rather than guessing.

questions.q: What double standard does the writer identify in some adults' behaviour?
choices: They criticise young people's phone use while demanding immediate replies from them.
They expect teenagers to abandon all social media at home.
They assume school clubs need longer messages than families.
They prohibit group chats but require students to use emails.
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph names this conflict between criticism and expectation.

questions.q: Which principle best captures the author's final argument?
choices: People should always disable every read receipt.
The sender has a right to receive a prompt response.
A notification should convey technical information without becoming a measure of affection.
Blue ticks are accurate indicators of social commitment.
questions.explanation: The closing sentence separates message receipt from how much the reader cares.
